description: We process payments under contracts with large corporations and hold the money we receive from them before paying others. We sell this payment service only as part of a bundle with another product and do not market it on its own.
label: license_likely
why: California rejected both the payroll processing exemption and a public-interest exemption and said the service falls within the scope of the Money Transmission Act.

description: We operate Bitcoin ATM kiosks. A customer scans identification, puts in dollars, and gives a wallet address, and we send bitcoin from our own inventory straight to that wallet. We never hold crypto for customers.
label: unclear
why: California said selling bitcoin from own inventory at a kiosk is not money transmission, but FinCEN treats exchangers who sell virtual currency for dollars as money transmitters, so state and federal answers differ.

description: We run bitcoin kiosks in third-party retail stores. Customers can buy bitcoin with cash, and at some locations sell bitcoin back to us for cash. All the bitcoin we sell comes from our own inventory, and we deal only in bitcoin.
label: unclear
why: California said own-inventory kiosk buying and selling is not money transmission, but FinCEN treats exchangers as money transmitters, so state and federal answers differ.

description: We collect cash from Bitcoin ATM operators by armored courier, count it at our vault, and then send each operator the equivalent amount of bitcoin, minus fees, out of our own inventory.
label: unclear
why: California said this is not receiving money for transmission, but the activity sits next to FinCEN-regulated exchanger activity, so the federal answer may differ.

description: We act as a payment processor for merchants that accept digital assets from customers and settle with them.
label: unclear
why: California said licensing was not required at this time but declined to decide whether digital-asset payment processing is receiving money for transmission or whether the agent-of-payee exemption would apply.

description: Our platform sends payroll advances to employees out of our own funds. The employer later repays us by turning the advance into a deduction from the employee's next paycheck.
label: unclear
why: California held the payroll processing exemption does not cover transferring advances to individuals. The excerpt does not show whether the advance model, which is lending, still needs a transmitter license.

description: We process card payments for online merchants under agreements with the merchants and with the card companies. For two card brands our setup meets all four of FinCEN's payment processor conditions, but for a third card brand it meets only three of the four.
label: license_likely
why: California published this opinion as 'not exempt as agent of payee or factoring'. The excerpt did not show the full analysis, so the conclusion rests on the published title.

description: We provide bill-payment software to money transmitters and to billers, and we act as an agent for each under our agreements. When a transmitter pays our invoice, we receive money but keep it as reimbursement, not passing it on to anyone.
label: likely_exempt
why: The software company itself was not engaged in money transmission because it kept the funds as reimbursement, though the transmitter on the other side stays regulated.

description: We run corporate reward programs where recipients can pick a gift card or a donation to a nonprofit. We hold client money in our operating account, and donations chosen by recipients are moved to a nonprofit ledger and sent to the charities every week.
label: license_likely
why: California disagreed that the nonprofit donation activity is exempt from the Money Transmission Act.

description: In our rewards product, donations that a recipient picks for a nonprofit are moved to a custodial bank account used only for those donations. Our agreement with each charity names us as its agent, says our receipt counts as receipt by the charity, and requires us to pass on every dollar we collect.
label: likely_exempt
why: After the agreement was revised to name the company as the nonprofit's agent, California found the donation activity met the agent-of-payee exemption.

description: We process donations for charities. Each charity's terms appoint us as its payment processing agent for a limited purpose and say a donor's payment to us counts as received by the charity.
label: unclear
why: California declined to opine on whether this fits the agent-of-payee exemption, saying it planned to propose regulations on the exemption.

description: We take payments in dollars from customers of hotels and other merchants, exchange the money for bitcoin, and send the bitcoin to the merchant, keeping a fee. The merchants want to be paid in something other than their local currency.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN ruled the company would be an exchanger of virtual currency and therefore a money transmitter. The payment-processor exemption did not apply because the system does not run only through BSA-regulated clearing and settlement systems.

description: We are building an online exchange where people trade a convertible virtual currency for dollars and for other virtual currencies. We match buyers and sellers and handle the settlement.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN ruled that a company setting up a virtual currency trading platform is a money transmitter, as it accepts and transmits value that substitutes for currency.

description: Our app lets customers hold bitcoin in an online wallet that we host. We store their coins, receive coins on their behalf, and send coins to other people whenever they tell us to.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats a hosted wallet provider as a money transmitter: the host is the transmitter and the wallet is the account.

description: We make wallet software that customers install and run themselves. Customers hold their own keys, and we never take custody of their coins or move them. We charge a license fee for the software.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats unhosted wallet providers as outside the money transmitter definition.

description: We mine a virtual currency on our own computers and keep the coins for our own use. Sometimes we convert some of them to dollars, but only for our own needs and never as a service to anyone else.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN ruled that mining solely for one's own purposes makes the miner a user, not a money transmitter.

description: We build our own software to buy virtual currency from sellers and resell it when our own investment decisions say so. We trade only for our own account and never for customers.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN ruled that producing and distributing the software, and trading virtual currency solely for the company's own investment, does not make a company a money transmitter.

description: We run an online exchange where customers around the world, including customers in the US, trade virtual currency and fiat money. We are based outside the US and have never registered as a money services business.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN assessed a civil penalty of more than $110 million for operating as an unregistered money services business.

description: We run a peer-to-peer marketplace where users buy and sell bitcoin from each other using many payment methods. We registered as a money services business years ago but let the registration lapse for several years.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN found the platform is a money services business and penalized it for failing to keep its registration, along with AML program and SAR failures.

description: We sell our own virtual currency to buyers for dollars as part of our business, and we have not registered with FinCEN as a money services business.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN assessed a $700,000 civil penalty against the company for failing to register as a money services business.

description: Our mobile app lets tens of millions of consumers spend, send, store, and invest money. We are licensed as a money transmitter by states, but our anti-money-laundering compliance program fell short of the requirements.
label: license_likely
why: Already a licensed money transmitter. 48 state regulators fined the company $80 million for BSA/AML failures, showing this model sits squarely inside state money transmission regulation.

description: Our app lets customers in California send money to Nigeria and other countries. We list ourselves with FinCEN as a foreign exchange dealer and a money transmitter, but we hold no California license.
label: license_likely
why: California ordered the company to stop transmitting money in California without a license after it carried out eight transfers from California to Nigeria.

description: Our website advertises our money transfer products, and we serve customers in California without holding a California license.
label: license_likely
why: California issued a desist and refrain order because the company advertised and provided money transmission in California with no license and was not an agent of a licensee.

description: We offer money transfers from Washington State to The Gambia so customers can send money to family and friends. We moved money for many consumers in California without a California license.
label: license_likely
why: California ordered the company to stop engaging in or advertising money transmission in California until licensed.

description: We are a New Hampshire company that has moved money for 26 California customers in at least 42 separate transactions since 2017. We do not hold a California license.
label: license_likely
why: California ordered the company to stop money transmission in the state because it never obtained a license.

description: Our website invites customers to receive money from anyone, anywhere, using just a username. We hold no California money transmitter license and are not an agent of a licensee.
label: license_likely
why: California ordered the company to stop engaging in and advertising money transmission in the state.

description: We help busy families and retirees keep up with their bills. Each month the customer gives us one lump sum by check or cash, and we mail checks to their landlord, utility and car lender on the due dates. We do not negotiate with the creditors.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN ruled this is money transmission: it just accepts funds and sends them to creditors, with no separate service that the transfer is integral to.

description: Our platform lets businesses and consumers pay each other online. A buyer funds an account by ACH, card or wire and later releases the money to the seller, who can leave the balance with us or withdraw it by ACH, wire or check. We do not check whether the terms of the sale were met.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN confirmed this payment platform is a money transmitter; the transfers are not integral to any other service, and there is no escrow-style verification.

description: We run an online exchange. Customers deposit dollars into accounts with us, and our matching system pairs people who want to buy bitcoin with people who want to sell it, then settles the trades between them.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN found two money transmissions occur in every trade on a virtual currency trading platform with pre-funded customer accounts.

description: We let hotels in Latin America get paid in bitcoin. The traveler pays us by credit card, and we convert that money into bitcoin and send it to the hotel.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN ruled the company accepts real currency and converts it to virtual currency for transmission to the merchant, so it is a money transmitter.

description: Our app keeps customers' cryptocurrency in accounts that we hold for them. Customers tell us to send it to other people's addresses or to sell it, and we carry out the instruction.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats the provider of a hosted (custodial) crypto wallet as a money transmitter.

description: I buy and sell bitcoin for people who find me through online ads. They pay me with cash or bank transfers, and I send them bitcoin or the reverse. I have done well over a thousand of these trades.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN penalized an individual peer-to-peer bitcoin exchanger for acting as an unregistered money transmitter.

description: We run cryptocurrency kiosks in many states, some of them in Texas. Customers insert cash to buy crypto, including a dollar-pegged stablecoin, and can also sell crypto back at the kiosk.
label: license_likely
why: The Texas Department of Banking ordered a kiosk operator for conducting money transmission in Texas through stablecoin transactions without a license.

description: Our marketplace connects U.S. clients with freelancers overseas. Clients pay through our site and we use licensed payment partners to send the money on to the freelancer abroad. Our terms of use only let us charge the client's payment method; they do not say we collect money on the freelancer's behalf.
label: license_likely
why: California DFPI found this marketplace receives money for transmission and does not qualify for the agent-of-the-payee exemption because its terms lacked the required agency language.

description: Our service buys bitcoin from shoppers with their dollars and then uses it to pay online merchants for the shopper's purchase. The shopper never handles the bitcoin.
label: license_likely
why: FinCEN's virtual currency guidance says a business that buys or sells convertible virtual currency for currency, including when intermediating between a buyer and a seller of goods, is a money transmitter.

description: We provide escrow for online sales of goods and services. We hold the buyer's payment, confirm that both sides did what the sale agreement required, and only then release the money to the seller or refund the buyer.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN found the money movement is integral to a real escrow service (acting as independent arbiter), so not a money transmitter.

description: We offer secured-transaction services for online sales. We hold the buyer's payment while the seller delivers and the buyer accepts the goods or services, then we release it. Moving the money is just one part of managing the transaction.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN found the acceptance and transmission of funds was not a separate service from the underlying transaction management, so not a money transmitter.

description: We rent powerful computers to customers who use them to mine cryptocurrency. Whatever the customers mine stays with them. We only charge rent for the machines.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN found that renting mining computer systems to others is not money transmission.

description: We run an armored car service that picks up customers' coins and bulk cash and delivers the exchanged currency back to them. In effect our armored cars act as remote teller counters.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN concluded this armored car coin and currency exchange service is not a money transmitter.

description: We are an investment firm. Using our own software, we buy bitcoin from sellers and resell it when we decide, strictly for our own account. We do not trade for customers and do not send anyone else's money.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN found that writing the software and investing in virtual currency for your own account is not money transmission.

description: We run a website where lenders fund small loans to entrepreneurs in developing countries. Local microfinance partners pre-screen the borrowers and upload their profiles, and we pass the lenders' money to the partners to fund the loans.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN found the fund transfers were integral to executing the micro-lending, so the company was not a money transmitter.

description: We are a debt management company. We negotiate lower balances and payment terms with a customer's creditors, and the plan is binding on both sides. We collect the customer's monthly payment and distribute it to the creditors under that plan.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN treated payments made under a negotiated, binding debt management plan as integral to the service, not money transmission.

description: We process payments for online merchants. With the customer's authorization we pull the money from their bank account by ACH into our account and then pass it on to the merchant. We work for the merchant, not the customer.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN's merchant payment processor ruling found this narrow ACH model is not money transmission.

description: We collect bill payments from a utility company's customers under a contract that names us as the utility's collection agent. We receive the payments on the utility's behalf and pass them on to it.
label: likely_exempt
why: FinCEN found a contracted utility collection agent close enough to the merchant payment processor ruling to avoid money transmitter status.

description: Our platform lets bands sell merchandise to their fans. Under a written agreement, we collect the fans' payments as the band's agent and forward the money to the band minus our fee. A fan's payment to us counts as payment to the band.
label: likely_exempt
why: California found this is money transmission but is exempt under the agent-of-the-payee exemption because of the written agency contract.

description: We run an online marketplace where travel operators list trips. Our terms appoint us as each operator's limited payment collection agent, so a traveler's payment to us counts as payment to the operator. A licensed payment company does the actual transfer, including to operators abroad.
label: likely_exempt
why: California DFPI found the marketplace exempt as an agent of the payee, even though it uses a licensed transmitter to move the funds.

description: Our software lets U.S. employers pay wages and benefits to employees who live in Mexico. We collect the payroll funds from the employer, a licensed partner converts the dollars to pesos, and we deliver the money to the employees' Mexican bank accounts.
label: likely_exempt
why: California DFPI found this falls under the payroll processing exemption.

description: We make a video game with two in-game currencies. One is earned by playing and the other is bought with dollars. Neither can be cashed out, transferred to other players, or used for anything except buying items from us inside the game.
label: likely_exempt
why: California found closed-loop in-game currency that can only be spent with the issuer is not money transmission.

description: Our game has a marketplace where players sell digital characters to each other for dollars. A separate licensed payment company handles the buyer's card and moves the money to the seller's account. We only collect a platform fee.
label: likely_exempt
why: California found the game company does not receive money for transmission when a separate licensed transmitter handles the funds.

description: Players of our game also sell their digital assets on outside marketplaces such as eBay. The marketplace's processor sends the sale proceeds to us, we keep our commission, and we credit the rest to the seller's account with us. Our terms say we collect the money as the seller's agent.
label: unclear
why: California DFPI said it was unclear whether the agent-of-the-payee exemption applies when two intermediaries are in the payment chain, and declined to opine.

description: We give online merchants in China a U.S. bank account number to use on big American marketplaces. The marketplaces pay their sales proceeds into it, and each day we move the dollars to an omnibus account in Hong Kong, where a partner converts them and pays the merchant's own account.
label: unclear
why: California DFPI declined to say whether the agent-of-the-payee exemption applies to this cross-border settlement service.

description: Our app lets users send bitcoin and other cryptocurrency to each other. We never touch dollars or dollar-backed stablecoins; we only relay the crypto from one user to another.
label: unclear
why: Under Texas policy, transmitting non-stablecoin crypto alone is not money transmission, but FinCEN treats accepting and transmitting convertible virtual currency as money transmission. The answer depends on jurisdiction.

description: We invest in bitcoin for our own account. Occasionally, when a trading counterparty or a creditor asks us to, we send bitcoin or dollars straight to a third party they name instead of back to them.
label: unclear
why: FinCEN said pure own-account investing is not money transmission, but transfers to third parties at a counterparty's direction should be closely scrutinized because they may be.

description: We offer multi-signature crypto wallets. We provide the wallet software and a second authorization key; a transaction needs both the customer's key and ours to be completed.
label: unclear
why: FinCEN's 2019 guidance says a multi-signature wallet provider may or may not be a money transmitter depending on whether it is hosted or un-hosted and who controls the funds.

description: Our platform lets customers swap one cryptocurrency for another, and sometimes for a dollar-pegged stablecoin. We do not hold dollars, and customers keep their coins in their own wallets until a swap runs.
label: unclear
why: Texas says stablecoin transactions may or may not be money transmission depending on how the stablecoin is handled, while FinCEN's exchanger rules are broader. The answer depends on jurisdiction and handling.
